Data Analytics Projects

📣 Marketing & Growth Analytics

Marketing performance, acquisition cost and customer lifetime value across channels.

MYSQLSQLPOWER BIPYTHON (VALIDATION)

Marketing Performance, Customer Acquisition & Lifetime Value Analytics

End-to-end analysis of 7 channels, 220 campaigns and 185K records, from raw CSV extracts to a MySQL star schema and a four-page Power BI dashboard, evaluating CAC, LTV, ROAS, funnel drop-off and retention.

Key result LTV < CAC Every ₹1 of spend returned ₹0.39 of attributed revenue (ROAS 0.39)

Business Impact: LTV:CAC is below 1 in all seven channels and ROI is −0.61, so the acquisition model does not currently recover its cost on recorded revenue. Only Affiliate is clearly weaker; fix measurement before moving budget.

GitHub

Business problem

Does marketing spend buy customers who are worth what they cost? Seven channels and 220 campaigns were generating spend, but there was no consistent view of what a customer costs, what a customer is worth, and where prospects are lost. First: can CAC, LTV, ROAS and retention be defined consistently enough to compare channels?

Key metrics

₹230.1Mmarketing spend, vs ₹89.2M attributed revenue
0.39blended ROAS (0.36–0.42 in every channel); ROI −0.61
₹74.8KCAC, vs ≈ ₹10K observed revenue per customer
< 1LTV : CAC in all 7 channels (0.09–0.16)
99.6%of leads do not appear as customers (3,075 acquired)
86.4%of customers have an event after day 30

Data, cleaning & analysis

Six raw CSV extracts (185,219 rows, Jan 2023 to Jul 2026) cleaned in MySQL, modelled as a star schema and reported in Power BI (12-table model, 15 DAX measures); Python was used only for independent validation. Source system not documented; amounts are in the data’s rupee values with no currency conversion. “LTV” means observed revenue to date, not margin-based and not a forecast.

Cleaning
  • Standardised 22 channel-name variants into 7 channels and parsed four date formats; 435 blank signup dates went to an “unknown” date member
  • Stripped ₹ and $ symbols from spend (3,116 rows) and revenue (3,665 rows), with no FX conversion
  • De-duplicated customers (10,500 to 9,985), campaigns and transactions (58,310 to 58,000); negative spend was nulled, refunds were flagged and clicks above impressions were nulled instead of deleted
  • Kept the 9.9% of transactions (₹10.2M) with no campaign, excluded from ROAS and reported separately
  • Net effect: 910 of 185,219 rows (0.5%) removed, then modelled as a star schema (5 fact tables, 4 dimensions) with 3 materialised tables and 11 views
Analysis
  • Calculated CAC by channel with first-touch attribution, aggregating each fact table separately to avoid double counting
  • Compared observed LTV with CAC (LTV:CAC), and ROAS and ROI by channel, campaign type and campaign, using about 70 SQL queries (CTEs, window functions, recursive calendar)
  • Mapped funnel drop-off from impressions to clicks, leads and customers
  • Built a retention flag and a signup-month cohort matrix (M1–M4)
  • Re-computed every headline KPI in Python (exact match) and tested channel differences with ANOVA, chi-square and bootstrap intervals

Dashboard

Power BI · 4 pages. Select a screenshot to enlarge it.

Key insights

Insight 1. Recorded revenue is well below marketing spend.

₹230.1M of spend produced ₹89.2M of attributed revenue (₹99.4M including unattributed). Blended ROAS is 0.39, no campaign reaches ROAS 1 (the highest is 0.96), and monthly ROAS exceeded 1 in only 4 of 43 months, all with low spend.

₹230.1M marketing spend
₹89.2M attributed revenue

What it means: Spend has not been returned in revenue anywhere in the portfolio. Revenue is not profit and only revenue to date is observed, so this is a gap to explain, not proof that marketing destroys value.

Insight 2. Acquisition cost is roughly seven to eight times the value each customer has generated.

Observed LTV:CAC is 0.094 to 0.157, below 1 in all seven channels. Customers average 5.8 transactions of about ₹1,714, so covering a ₹74.8K CAC would take roughly 44.

₹74.8K CAC
≈ ₹10K revenue per customer to date

What it means: Because LTV is observed rather than forecast, a longer horizon would raise it, but retention alone cannot be assumed to close a gap this size. Acquisition cost, value per customer and data completeness need review first.

Insight 3. Affiliate is the one clearly weaker channel.

Affiliate has the highest CAC (₹86.7K), the lowest observed LTV (₹8.2K) and LTV:CAC of 0.094, taking 12.5% of spend for 10.8% of acquired customers. Its bootstrap interval (0.081–0.109) does not overlap Referral’s (0.135–0.182), but the other five channels overlap and ANOVA on revenue per customer gives p = 0.27.

What it means: Affiliate is the strongest candidate for review. A ranking-only view would have wrongly recommended scaling Referral.

Insight 4. The funnel loses nearly everything between lead and customer.

198.8M impressions produce 6.49M clicks, 0.76M leads and 3,075 customers. CTR is uniform across channels (3.19–3.32%), click-to-lead is 11.72% and lead-to-customer is 0.40%.

0.76M leads
3,075 customers

What it means: The loss is downstream (sales process, lead quality or tracking), not in channel choice. Leads and customers share no ID, so the exact stage cannot be located.

Insight 5. Spend is spread thinly, and customer value is concentrated.

The top five of 220 campaigns hold only 5.47% of spend (2.3% would be uniform). On the customer side, median revenue is ₹4,075 against a mean of ₹9,954, and the top 10% of customers generate 48.6% of revenue.

5.47% of spend in the top 5 campaigns
48.6% of revenue from the top 10% of customers

What it means: There is no small set of campaigns to cut, and averages overstate the typical customer. Value segmentation would show where acquisition works.

Insight 6. The headline retention number is not monthly stickiness.

86.4% of customers have at least one event after day 30, but only about a quarter of each signup cohort is active in a given month (M1–M4: 23.9–25.2%).

86.4% return at least once after day 30
≈ 24–25% active in a given month

What it means: A windowed, eligibility-adjusted measure is needed before retention drives decisions. This is correlation only.

Business impact

  • Acquisition economics. LTV:CAC is below 1 in all seven channels, blended ROAS is 0.39 and ROI is −0.61. The model does not currently recover its cost on recorded revenue.
  • Measurement and attribution. 9.9% of revenue (₹10.2M) has no campaign, and channel fields agree for only 14.8% of customers. Campaign and channel ROAS cannot be fully trusted yet.
  • Lead-to-customer conversion. 99.6% of leads do not appear as customers, in every channel. A downstream conversion or measurement issue, not a channel issue.
  • Affiliate. Highest CAC (₹86.7K) and lowest LTV:CAC (0.094). The priority channel for review against a holdout.
  • Customer value. The top 10% of customers generate 48.6% of revenue. Value-based segmentation matters more than the average customer.

No marketing decision was changed or tested in this project, so no financial outcome is claimed. The size of any improvement would need controlled testing.

Recommendations

  1. Fix measurement before moving budget. Agree one attribution rule (channel is defined three ways and agrees for only 14.8% of customers), report forecast LTV alongside observed LTV, and define retention at fixed 30/60/90-day windows.
  2. Review and test the Affiliate programme. Test a reduction or restructure against a holdout instead of shifting budget on channel rank alone.
  3. Investigate the lead-to-customer gap. Link lead IDs to CRM records and analyse Lead → MQL → SQL → Opportunity → Customer progression to find where 99.6% of leads are lost.
  4. Validate revenue attribution before campaign-level optimisation. 9.9% of revenue has no campaign, so capture an order-level campaign key and treat current campaign ROAS as descriptive.
  5. Segment customers by value and monitor reconciled KPIs. Add value-decile analysis and rebuild dashboard table totals as ratio measures so they tie to the SQL source.

Next steps: in 30 days, standardise attribution and re-export the dashboard; in 60 days, run the Affiliate holdout test and build windowed retention; in 90 days, run controlled budget experiments and reallocate only where results are statistically supported.

Limitations

  • Revenue is not profit, and LTV is observed revenue to date, not margin-based or a forecast.
  • Attribution and signup dates are unreliable: 9.9% of revenue has no campaign, about 89% of attributed transactions fall outside their campaign’s dates, and about half of dated events precede the recorded signup date.
  • CAC, retention and LTV:CAC use the first-touch campaign channel, “Average LTV by channel” uses the CRM channel, and ROAS uses the channel on each transaction.
  • Apart from Affiliate vs Referral, channel differences are within sampling variation; some Power BI table totals still add up row-level ratios.
  • No currency conversion was applied, and the dataset’s origin is undocumented.

👥 Customer & Retention Analytics

Customer-focused analytics covering churn definitions, revenue exposure and early-warning signals.

SQLPYTHONMYSQLPOWER BI

SaaS Customer Churn & Retention Analytics

Validated 5 tables (500 accounts, 33.1K records), found that two sources disagree on who churned (110 vs 352), and built a 5-page Power BI dashboard.

Key result 110 vs 352 customers flagged as churned by the two sources (70.4% on the events table)

Business Impact: Revenue reporting: One agreed churn definition is needed before revenue at risk is quoted.

GitHub

Business problem

Which customers are leaving, why, how much recurring revenue is exposed, and who needs attention? First: is churn defined and measured consistently?

Key metrics

70.4%customers with a churn event (352 of 500; 95% CI 66.3–74.2%)
110 vs 352customers marked churned by the account flag vs the churn events table
$238.6KMRR at risk: 19 active customers with low usage and 5+ tickets
$3.02MActive MRR, against $10.16M of open MRR across all accounts

Data, cleaning & analysis

Synthetic data; source and licence are undocumented. Findings are associations in a simulated dataset.

Cleaning
  • Found two churn sources that disagree: 110 customers flagged in accounts vs 352 with churn events. The events table was used as the source of truth and the choice documented
  • Found all 352 churned accounts still hold open subscriptions ($7.14M of $10.16M open MRR), so “Active” KPIs exclude them
  • Mapped usage to accounts through subscriptions and aggregated every table to one row per customer before joining (500 rows × 38 columns)
  • No rows were deleted or imputed; 41.2% of satisfaction scores stay missing
Analysis
  • Measured churn by plan, industry, channel, tenure, usage and tickets, plus cohort retention and revenue concentration
  • Scored active customers with a transparent points-based risk heuristic and listed the top 15 for outreach
  • Tested every segment difference: Wilson interval, chi-square, Fisher exact (with Bonferroni) and Mann–Whitney
  • Reported the results in a five-page Power BI dashboard with five slicers

Dashboard

Power BI · 5 pages. Select a screenshot to enlarge it.

Key insights

Insight 1. Churn is widespread, but its definition is unsettled.

352 of 500 customers (70.4%) have a churn event, yet the accounts file flags only 110, and every churned account still has an open subscription.

110 flagged churned in accounts.csv
352 with a churn event in churn.csv

What it means: The metric is “ever churned in two years”, not a period rate. Churn and revenue at risk cannot be reported with confidence until the sources are reconciled.

Insight 2. Revenue churn is 10.4% or about 70%, depending on the source.

10.4% on a subscription-end basis ($1.18M of $11.34M ever billed), but about 70% on a churn-event basis ($7.99M).

10.4% revenue churn, subscription basis
≈ 70% revenue churn, churn-event basis

What it means: The two figures answer different questions and must not be compared; finance needs to confirm the authoritative source.

Insight 3. Usage and ticket volume do not distinguish churners.

Churn is 71.3% / 71.9% / 68.1% for High / Low / Medium usage (p = 0.72), and churned customers average 3.96 tickets against 4.09 for active ones (p = 0.63).

What it means: A “low usage” or “many tickets” alert alone would not find churners in this data; richer signals would need testing.

Insight 4. Segment differences are mostly within noise; only Ads stands out, tentatively.

Churn by plan, industry and channel is not reliably different (p = 0.68 / 0.79 / 0.14). Ads is 60.2% against 72.9% for the rest (p = 0.019, but 0.093 after adjustment).

72.9% churn, all other channels
60.2% churn, Ads (n = 98)

What it means: No plan or industry deserves its own retention programme on churn rate alone. Ads is a hypothesis to test, not a reason to reallocate spend.

Insight 5. Churn is highest among the newest customers (an association).

82.9% at 0–3 months, then 73.9%, 71.4% and 53.9% at 12+ months (n = 152 / 88 / 119 / 141).

82.9% churn, 0–3 months tenure
53.9% churn, 12+ months tenure

What it means: Consistent with an onboarding risk, but tenure is measured differently for churned and active customers, so it needs a time-to-event analysis before it is called a driver.

Business impact

  • Revenue reporting. $7.14M of the $10.16M open MRR sits with accounts that have a churn event; Active MRR is $3.02M. One agreed churn definition is needed before revenue at risk is quoted.
  • Early-warning alerts. Churn is 68–72% in every usage bucket, and ticket volume does not separate churners. Alerts on usage or tickets alone would not find churners.
  • Early customer life. 82.9% churn at 0–3 months against 53.9% at 12+ months. Onboarding is the place to investigate, once sized properly.
  • Customer Success focus. 19 customers carry $238.6K of MRR with low usage and 5+ tickets. A short triage list, with outcomes tracked to validate it.

MRR at risk is exposure, not a forecast of lost revenue. The data is synthetic and has no outcome data, so no financial impact is claimed.

Recommendations

  1. Agree one churn definition and report revenue churn on a labelled basis. Reconcile billing with finance, treat reactivations explicitly, and publish both the 10.4% and the ≈ 70% until the source is settled.
  2. Review onboarding and the first 90 days. Size the effect with a time-to-event analysis first (82.9% churn at 0–3 months).
  3. Do not base retention triggers on usage or ticket volume alone. Test recency, trend, feature-level usage and escalations, and back-test any score on a hold-out period.
  4. Use the 19-customer at-risk list for triage and improve churn-reason capture. Track what happens to listed accounts, and note that 15.8% of churn reasons are “unknown”.

Limitations

  • Synthetic, observational data: associations only, and none establishes cause.
  • “Churned” means “ever had a churn event”; KPI bases differ, and current_plan matches the latest subscription for only 37% of accounts.
  • The risk score and MRR at risk are unvalidated heuristics, and the .pbix and DAX are not available.

🛒 Sales & Profitability Analytics

Sales analytics linking discounting, regions and products to profit, plus customer segmentation.

SQLPYTHONMYSQLTABLEAU

Superstore Sales & Profitability Analytics

Cleaned 10K sales records, linked discount levels to profit and segmented 793 customers with RFM.

Key result −119.20% margin at 50%+ discount (29.51% at 0% discount)

Business Impact: Deep-discount lines (30%+): A concentrated source of margin leakage.

GitHub

Business problem

Where does a multi-category retailer make money, where does it lose it, and how much of that is explained by discounting?

Key metrics

$2.30Mtotal sales, Jan 2014 – Dec 2017
12.47%overall profit margin ($286.4K profit)
−0.864correlation between discount and line margin
793customers segmented with RFM

Data, cleaning & analysis

Public Sample Superstore dataset (Tableau sample data): it has no product-cost or shipping-cost fields and is not a real business.

Cleaning
  • Validated all 9,994 lines (dates, Quantity > 0, Sales ≥ 0, 0 ≤ Discount ≤ 1): no nulls or duplicates, so no rows were removed
  • Kept the 1,871 loss-making lines (18.7%) as genuine losses; no outliers were removed
  • Order-level totals repeat on each line ($7.11M if summed vs the true $2.30M), so KPIs use line-level values
  • Engineered line-level margin and seven discount buckets in Python, then loaded MySQL with six SQL views that feed Tableau
Analysis
  • Defined margin as a ratio of sums and grouped discounts into buckets to show where profit disappears
  • Used CTEs with LAG() for year-over-year growth, and HAVING to list loss-making sub-categories and states
  • Split the 49 states into a sales-vs-profit quadrant to find high-sales, low-profit states
  • Segmented 793 customers with RFM and joined the segments back to transactions

Dashboard

Tableau · 5 dashboards. Select a screenshot to enlarge it.

Key insights

Insight 1. Margin falls steadily as the discount deepens.

Margin runs from 29.51% at 0% discount to −119.20% at 50%+, turning negative from the 21–30% bucket; the correlation with discount is −0.864. This is an association: the data does not show the extra volume discounts brought in.

29.51% margin at 0% discount
−119.20% margin at 50%+ discount

What it means: Above roughly 20% discount the business is paying customers to take the product: at 50%+ off, every $100 of sales loses about $119.

Insight 2. A small share of deep-discount lines explains a net loss.

Lines discounted 30%+ are 13.9% of order lines and 15.8% of sales, yet net −$135,376. The common 20% discount still earns 11.58%.

21.80% margin on lines below 30% discount
−37.32% margin on lines at 30%+ discount

What it means: The problem is the deep end of the discount range, not discounting in general.

Insight 3. Tables lose money despite high sales.

Tables lose $17,725 on $206,966 of sales (average discount 26.13%); Bookcases and Supplies also lose. Furniture’s margin is 2.49% against 17.40% for Technology.

What it means: Ranking by sales would reward Tables. Without cost data, discounting and product cost cannot be separated.

Insight 4. The Central-region profit gap sits in two states.

West earns $108,418 against $39,706 in Central. Texas (−$25,729) and Illinois (−$12,608), with average discounts of 37–39%, lose $38,337 combined.

31.11% margin in the rest of Central
−15.31% margin in Texas + Illinois

What it means: Read it as “two heavily discounted states underperform”: a region-wide fix would be mis-targeted.

Insight 5. 2017 growth was real but turned into less profit.

Sales grew 20.36% but profit only 14.24%. Margin slipped from 13.43% to 12.74% as orders rose from 1,315 to 1,687 and average order value fell.

+20.36% sales growth in 2017
+14.24% profit growth in 2017

What it means: Growth came from more, smaller orders at a slightly lower margin; the cause is not isolated in this analysis.

Insight 6. Customer count and customer value do not line up.

“Lost” is the largest RFM group by headcount (297 customers), but “Loyal” is the most valuable (211 customers, $716,805 of sales).

What it means: Size retention and win-back effort by value, not headcount. The At Risk figure ($309,502) is historical spend, not recoverable revenue.

Business impact

  • Deep-discount lines (30%+). −$135,376 on 1,393 lines (13.9% of lines); all other lines earn +$421,773 (21.80% margin). A concentrated source of margin leakage.
  • Texas + Illinois. −$38,337 on $250,354 of sales; the rest of Central earns +$78,044. Two states drive the Central loss.
  • Tables. −$17,725 on $206,966 of sales. A high-revenue line that reduces total profit.
  • 2017 growth quality. Sales +20.36% but profit +14.24%; margin 13.43% to 12.74%. Growth added less profit per sales dollar.

These overlap (the same deep-discount lines drive the state and product losses), so they must not be added together. Figures are observed 2014–2017 history; no change was implemented, so no profit improvement is claimed.

Recommendations

  1. Introduce discount governance by sub-category. Set ceilings with approval above them, starting with Binders (37.23% average discount), Machines (30.61%), Tables (26.13%) and Bookcases (21.11%), and track the 30%+ discount share of sales (15.8% today).
  2. Review Tables at SKU level. 55.2% of Tables lines carry a 30%+ discount and net −$30,698, while the rest earn +$12,973; test price floors for the worst SKUs.
  3. Focus the Central review on Texas and Illinois. 43.5% of their lines carry a 30%+ discount; check approval practices and product mix before changing regional strategy.
  4. Prioritise retention by value and track growth together with margin. Target At Risk and high-value Loyal customers first, and test any change against a control group.

Limitations

  • No product-cost or shipping-cost fields, and the dataset is a public sample, so Profit is used as supplied.
  • The discount–profit result is an association; no experiment or controlled regression was run, and RFM segments are rule-based.
  • Some Tableau panels are known to be wrong (flagged in the captions); the figures quoted here are the correct ones.

🧑‍💼 People & HR Analytics

Workforce analytics focused on attrition drivers and where to act first.

PYTHONSQLMYSQLPOWER BIDAX

Employee Attrition Analytics

Analyzed 1,470 employees (16.12% attrition), tested 4 hypotheses and ranked the drivers with a logistic regression model.

Key result 30.5% vs 10.4% attrition with vs without overtime (16.12% overall)

Business Impact: Overtime: An actionable lever, and the first place to pilot a change.

GitHub

Business problem

Why are employees leaving, which segments face higher attrition risk, and where should retention effort be focused?

Key metrics

16.12%attrition: 237 of 1,470 employees left
30.5% vs 10.4%attrition with vs without overtime
43%of exits come from the 23% of staff with 0–2 years of tenure
0.81ROC-AUC of the driver model (recall 0.34)

Data, cleaning & analysis

Public IBM HR Analytics dataset. It has no dates, so there is no trend, no annualised turnover and no voluntary/involuntary split.

Cleaning
  • The data arrived structurally clean (0 missing values, no duplicates or disguised nulls); dropped 3 zero-variance columns (35 → 32)
  • Validated ranges and cross-field rules (tenure ≤ working years ≤ age − 18): 0 violations
  • Tested IQR outlier trimming and rejected it: it keeps only 699 of 1,470 rows and removes every performance-rating-4 row
  • Loaded the cleaned file into MySQL for independent KPI checks, and built age, tenure, income and distance bands
Analysis
  • Tested four hypotheses (early-career, low pay, overtime and travel, level and tenure): three supported, one partly
  • Cross-checked the attrition KPIs in SQL, and separated volume (how many leave) from risk (the rate)
  • Checked group differences with chi-square and Mann–Whitney tests, and showed that age, tenure, level and pay overlap
  • Ranked the drivers jointly with a logistic regression (80/20 split), judged on recall and not accuracy alone

Dashboard

Power BI · 2 pages. Select a screenshot to enlarge it.

Key insights

Insight 1. Overtime is the sharpest single signal.

127 of 416 employees on overtime left, against 110 of 1,054 without it. The gap holds at every job level, and overtime is the largest positive coefficient in the model.

10.4% attrition without overtime
30.5% attrition with overtime

What it means: Overtime is not just a proxy for junior roles, and management can change it. Only a pilot can tell burnout from other differences.

Insight 2. Attrition is concentrated in the first two years.

Tenure of 0–2 years has 29.8% attrition against 8.1% at 10+ years. Employees under 25 leave at 39.2%, and job level 1 at 26.3%.

23% of staff have 0–2 years of tenure
43% of all exits come from them

What it means: Age, tenure and level overlap, so this is one early-career signal, not three independent ones.

Insight 3. Volume and risk point to different roles.

R&D has 56% of exits but the lowest department rate (13.84%). Sales Representative has the highest role rate (39.76%, 33 of 83) and Research Director the lowest (2.50%).

What it means: Prioritise by rate and headcount together; small groups make single percentages imprecise.

Insight 4. Low pay is associated with attrition, mostly at the bottom of the scale.

The lowest income quartile leaves at 29.3% against 10.3% in the highest. Median monthly income is 3,202 for leavers and 5,204 for stayers.

29.3% lowest income quartile
10.3% highest income quartile

What it means: Pay overlaps with seniority (income–level correlation 0.95), so benchmark pay within each level instead of giving across-the-board raises.

Insight 5. The model ranks drivers but cannot flag individuals.

Logistic regression reaches 86.05% accuracy against an 84.0% always-“stays” baseline, with recall 0.34 and ROC-AUC 0.81.

84.0% always-“stays” baseline accuracy
86.05% model accuracy (recall 0.34)

What it means: Use it to confirm which factors matter and in which direction, not to single out employees.

Business impact

  • Overtime. 30.5% attrition with overtime against 10.4% without, at every job level. An actionable lever, and the first place to pilot a change.
  • Early tenure. 43% of exits come from the 23% of staff with 0–2 years of tenure. The largest pool of leavers sits early in the employee lifecycle.
  • Role risk vs volume. R&D has 56% of exits but the lowest rate; Sales Representatives have the highest (39.8%). Target by rate and headcount together.
  • Pay at the bottom. The lowest income quartile leaves at 29.3%, against about 10.5% in the top half. Benchmark pay inside each level.

These are associations in one snapshot, not proof of cause. The data has no dates or cost-of-attrition figures, so no financial impact is claimed.

Recommendations

  1. Test overtime reduction where attrition is highest. Pilot an overtime cap or compensation change for one group (Laboratory Technicians 50.0% on overtime, Research Scientists 34.0%, Sales Executives 33.0%) and compare exits with a similar group without it.
  2. Prioritise early-tenure retention. Focus onboarding, mentoring and 6/12/24-month check-ins on job-level-1 and early-tenure employees.
  3. Review pay at the bottom of the scale. Benchmark level-1 and low-income, high-attrition roles against peers within each level, rather than adjusting pay across the board.
  4. Review travel load and monitor by rate and headcount. Frequent travellers leave at 24.9% against 8.0% for non-travellers; avoid scoring individuals on gender, age or marital status.

Limitations

  • One snapshot with no dates and no cost-of-attrition data, so there is no trend and no financial impact estimate.
  • Associations only: overtime, tenure, pay and level are correlated, so confounding is possible and causal claims need a pilot.
  • Model recall is 0.34 on a single train/test split (47 leavers in the test set), and some dashboard count visuals do not reconcile.

🌱 Energy & Operations Analytics

Operational analytics of a solar plant: validating KPIs before reporting on performance.

PYTHONSQLMYSQLPOWER BIDAX

Solar Plant Performance & Efficiency Analytics

Validated the KPIs of a 22-inverter solar plant: caught a 24.7× energy overstatement and a constant “efficiency” ratio, then re-derived output and flagged 2 weak inverters.

Key result 5.38M vs 132.7M kWh validated plant energy vs the first-pass dashboard figure (24.7× overstated)

Business Impact: Energy reporting: Needs a reconciliation check before reporting.

GitHub

Business problem

How efficiently is the plant generating energy, where is it lost, and which inverters need attention? Each KPI must first be checked: does it vary, and does it reconcile?

Key metrics

≈ 5.38M kWhreconciled plant energy (≈ 158 MWh/day), three methods agree within 2%
24.7×overstatement of the original dashboard’s Total Energy (132.70M kWh)
−9.2% / −7.7%energy of two inverters against the fleet mean; the other 20 sit between −1.5% and +3.5%
63mid-day zero-output readings, about 0.3% of plant energy (estimated)

Data, cleaning & analysis

Kaggle Solar Power Generation dataset, Plant 1. It has no capacity, tariff, maintenance or alarm data, and the irradiation unit is assumed to be kW/m².

Cleaning
  • Parsed two timestamp formats, renamed the clashing SOURCE_KEY columns and joined readings with weather on (date_time, plant_id)
  • Kept only producing rows (DC > 0 and AC > 0): 31,951 rows removed, mostly night-time; no nulls, duplicates or negatives found
  • daily_yield is a cumulative counter, so energy is taken once per inverter-day; summing it row by row overstated energy 24.7×
  • The AC/DC ratio is a near-constant ≈ 0.098 (probable DC scale difference, unconfirmed), so it was flagged and not used to rank inverters
Analysis
  • Built first-pass KPIs in pandas, SQL and DAX, then validated each: does it vary, are the units sensible, does it reconcile independently
  • Reconciled plant energy three ways (inverter-day maxima, lifetime counter, integrated AC power), all within 2%
  • Compared inverters on energy against the fleet mean, weather-normalised output and how persistent the gap is
  • Counted mid-day zero-output readings (irradiation above 0.2 kW/m²) as candidate downtime

Dashboard

Power BI · 1 page. Select a screenshot to enlarge it.

Key insights

Insight 1. The plant produced about 5.38M kWh, not 132.7M.

Inverter-day maxima give 5,380,274 kWh, the lifetime counter 5,381,113 kWh and integrated AC power 5,292,514 kWh. Mean daily energy is 158,243 kWh, and the peak day is 193,764 kWh (20 May).

132.70M kWh dashboard Total Energy (summed counter)
5.38M kWh reconciled plant energy

What it means: Energy reporting needs a one-value-per-inverter-day definition and a reconciliation check.

Insight 2. The original efficiency and loss KPIs do not describe plant performance.

AC ÷ DC is about 0.098 for every inverter and every irradiation band (9.73% / 9.80% / 9.77%), and DC integrates to 54.1M kWh against 5.38M kWh recorded.

9.78% “efficiency” on the original dashboard
90.22% “loss”, which is just 100 minus efficiency

What it means: A “90% loss” must not be reported. The likely cause is a DC scale difference, which needs confirmation from the data provider.

Insight 3. Two inverters consistently deliver less than their peers.

bvBOhCH3iADSZry (−9.2%) and 1BY6WEcLGh8j5v7 (−7.7%) are below the fleet mean on 97% and 82% of days; the next inverter is at −1.5%. Together they sit about 41,208 kWh below the fleet mean over 34 days (0.77% of plant energy).

−1.5% to +3.5% the other 20 inverters
−9.2% and −7.7% the two flagged inverters

What it means: These are the first inspection candidates. The data has no maintenance or alarm information, so it cannot say why they are low.

Insight 4. Output follows sunshine, so comparisons must be weather-normalised.

Correlation of AC power with irradiation is 0.985, and daily plant energy against daily insolation is r = 0.88. Daily plant energy ranges from 118 to 194 MWh.

What it means: Raw output cannot judge performance; compare days, months and inverters on a weather-normalised basis.

Insight 5. Downtime is small, and the May-to-June decline is weather.

63 zero-AC readings occurred mid-day (32 on 7 June and 24 on 14 June), about 15,777 kWh (0.29% of energy, estimated). Average AC fell 6.2% from May to June while irradiation fell 8.7%.

What it means: Availability losses are small, and there is no evidence of degradation in 34 days (that needs at least 12 months of data).

Business impact

  • Energy reporting. Dashboard Total Energy was 132.70M kWh against a reconciled 5.38M kWh (24.7×). Needs a reconciliation check before reporting.
  • Efficiency and loss. AC/DC is about 0.098 everywhere, so “efficiency 9.78%” and “loss 90.22%” cannot separate inverters. Avoids acting on an artefact.
  • Inverter maintenance. Two of 22 inverters are 9.2% and 7.7% below the fleet mean (about 41,208 kWh over 34 days). A targeted inspection list, not a fleet-wide review.
  • Downtime. 63 mid-day zero readings, about 0.29% of plant energy (estimated), clustered on 7 and 14 June. Small, but two dates are worth checking against logs.

These are descriptive comparisons within one plant and period. There is no tariff or capacity data and the cause of the inverter gap is unknown, so no financial impact is claimed.

Recommendations

  1. Inspect bvBOhCH3iADSZry and 1BY6WEcLGh8j5v7 first. Collect alarm and maintenance logs and compare strings, soiling and shading with the other 20 inverters.
  2. Report plant energy with a reconciliation check. Replace the dashboard measures with the inverter-day definition and show the reconciliation to the lifetime counter.
  3. Stop reporting AC/DC efficiency and “loss” until DC units are confirmed. Meanwhile, monitor inverters on weather-normalised output and persistence.
  4. Check 7 and 14 June in the operations logs, and gather at least 12 months of data before drawing degradation conclusions.

Limitations

  • Only 34 days, one plant and one weather sensor, with no capacity, tariff or maintenance data, so financial impact and causes cannot be assessed.
  • The DC power scale is unconfirmed, and the analysis is descriptive: no statistical tests or predictive models.
  • The Power BI file and screenshot still show the original KPI definitions.
